titleStmt.title: Interview with Joseph John Dvorabic, July 31, 2003
titleStmt.author: Thomas A. Swope

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph John Dvorabic was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Joseph John Dvorabic. Mr. Dvorabic served in the U.S. Army with the 143rd AAA Gun Battalion. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope. And this interview was recorded at Mr. Dvorabic's home in Euclid, Ohio on July 31st, 2003. Joe was 78 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I lived on Silsby Avenue in Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How old would you have been in '41? When were you born?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I was born in '25. So I was 18 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Or actually in '41 you would have been either 15 or 16, right?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Well, wait a minute. '41?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. You were born in '25. You were probably still in school.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Sixteen.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Still in high school?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. Sixteen.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yes. I remember it was a Sunday. I heard it on the news. And I was thinking, gee, here they're going to start drafting the boys. I figured, well, in two years it will be all over with. To my surprise, it wasn't over with.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I got drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did any of your classmates drop out of school and join?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. A lot of them did. But I wasn't in school at that time. I was working.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I left school when I was 16 and -- we had to get a job at home because nobody was working. And that's where -- where I ended up. I was working in the defense plants and they decided they needed me in the service. So that's when I went.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you had deferments from that job for a little while anyway, right?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Well, I wasn't old enough to be drafted at --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That, too. Sure.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: So until I was 18 and then that was draftable age then.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So when were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: July 26th, 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what was that like when you first had to report and you were thrown into basic training with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: It was a new experience. I think the biggest experience. I never had a train ride in my life until I left Cleveland to go to Columbus to Fort Hayes. And then they give me a real ride from Fort Hayes to California. Five days in on a train.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what else can you tell me about your basic training?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. We had basic training -- at that time anyone that was drafted that was 18 years of age, they said they had to be in this country one year before they were shipped out. Well, I left -- one year to the day when we left New York I was in this country.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: 26th day of July 1944, we left New York.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Anything unusual happen during your training time during that year?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Unusual?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Or interesting or funny.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. I got stuck out in the desert.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How did that happen?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Well, that -- in other words, we do our training out in the desert. The Mojave Desert. Unusual? Yeah. 120 degrees in the shade. We had Italian prisoners in our camp at that time. They had it made. I remember one thing unusual over there at Camp Irwin. And that was in Barstow, California. That they had a swimming pool out in that desert. The difference between the atmospheric pressure -- atmospheric temperature and the water so different that you could feel like you were jumping in ice water. We didn't use the pool at all. It was too cold.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Really. Wow.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: We did all our anti-aircraft shooting out at Camp Irwin. That was out in the desert. You could see why. When shells go out there, they don't go off. They're laying out in the desert.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the outfit?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I was a cannoneer. What I did is I operated a clock that traversed the gun from right to left. And I put that in order where it goes automatically or -- or I could do it manually.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And what was this outfit? Were you with the 143rd at that point?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yes. It was the 143rd Battery C.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Anti-aircraft gun battalion?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you shipped out in July of 1944, right?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: July 26th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I think it was 14 days. And we went over on an English ship because it just came back from South America. I guess they had mutton that they got there and they're bringing it back to England. That's the ship we were on. So we ate mutton three times a day. We didn't want to see mutton for a long time after that trip.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Anything else happen in that crossing?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I remember we were alerted a couple of times of the possibility of subs around, but we never saw anything or saw any action of it. That's the only thing that showed up. We were on duty to observe if there were any subs around, but we never saw any. But they said that they had alerted that there were some around. But the thing is that 14 days and we ended up in Liverpool, England or -- no. Yeah. Yes, it was Liverpool. Landed at Liverpool, England and then went down to Blackmore and -- it was on the border of England and Wales. We were there three weeks to get our equipment. And -- and that was our 90 millimeter gun and all our impregnated -- gas impregnated clothes. That took three weeks. And then we boarded a ship in South Hampton and over to Normandy. That took 12 hours. I remember we left at midnight and about 6:00 in the morning we hit the shore in Normandy. Well, I remember we had some clothing on that was -- that were impregnated for gas warfare. And I remember I had shoes on for a week. And it was that slimy stuff that was inside the shoes, as well as outside. We had -- had our feet in that for a week before we could change. But at the time we landed there, the beach was secure and there was no problems there, as far as landing. We hit the beach -- I think it was around 7:00 in the morning. And then we had to wait until the tide goes down. Well, we were on an LST. We hit the -- hit the shore and then we wait for the water to go down so we can pull our guns off the LST. We were a mobile outfit so that we had tractors pulling our guns. And so we got ashore then. That's -- actually, it was a really different world when you reach there. You say, where are you? All kinds of different languages and you can't understand people talking. But it was an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What beach did you land on?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Normandy.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you know which beach it was?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Omaha Beach.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Omaha, okay. All right.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Omaha Beach. Yeah, it was -- I think there was -- there was a whole battalion went there. And I think -- I think it was B Battery. They had to put them on Liberty Ship in order to bring them over. And we went on an LST. I don't know which is better, but I remember on the LST they had a big balloon up on top over there for strafing.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Because -- a big balloon up there so the planes wouldn't come down and strafe us. But we had no problems at all. I think the Germans didn't have enough planes to go there anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Okay. So did you have much contact with the French people when you got over there?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: No. We had a little trouble communicating, but you'll learn how in time. But, you know, the French people were real good to us at first and then it seemed to change. I don't know. They weren't as friendly as they were at first. Because when we got into Paris, it was only a week after Paris was liberated.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: And I remember the people all coming out when we drove through town. People all come out waving to you. But that didn't last long though. Why? I don't know. Well, they were -- there was enough war. I guess, they had enough of seeing the military people and -- but --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So did your unit set up then near Paris?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. We were -- C Battery was stationed -- we were basically set up to guard Paris for anti-aircraft attack. And we were at -- Battery C was in St Denis. That's north of Paris. Some of our outfits were stationed right into the center of a racetrack. They were set up there. But we encircled Paris and we were there to protect the city in case there were air attacks. But there wasn't any. I do remember one night that we were on alert that we heard planes overhead. And you can tell they weren't ours because of the sound of the engine. There weren't too many jet engines at that time. They were propeller-driven planes. And the sound of the engines you can tell that they were something else. I remember talking to Captain Kent on this and he was saying that they were dropping spies in there at that time into Paris and -- so he said he was on duty that night about shooting -- shooting them down, but we didn't shoot at all. So that was an experience in Paris.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How long were you there then in Paris?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I think -- about three months I think we were there. Maybe -- maybe not that long, but then we went up to Belgium. We set up through Liege. I guess that's what they call buzz bomb alley. Germans -- Germans were throwing buzz bombs. We used to see as many as five and six at a time coming overhead. And what didn't go -- drop off at Antwerp went over to England. I never saw them when we were in England. Well, we were only there three weeks. I never did see any buzz bombs over in England. But -- but you could see a lot of destruction. I think they used the -- the Germans used a V-1 rocket where you can't tell. The buzz bombs that they had, it was like a propeller-driven plane. It looked like a plane, but it had an engine out the back end and it just pushed it along. And when the gas ran down, it just tapered and went right down and that's where it landed. We saw a lot of them in Liege. And I think they -- they were basically going into Antwerp. Antwerp was the port where they would bring in food and troops and things like that. And they were trying to destroy that area. Well, they did a pretty good job at it, but they didn't. I remember there was a river from Antwerp all the way to Liege. All along the river, they -- they had supplies for the First Army there. And that's another thing that we were guarding. That they would -- airplane attack, but that never happened. I don't think the Germans had enough fuel or pilots to do the job. And -- yeah, we were in Liege there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were you allowed to shoot at these buzz bombs or did you --

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: No. They didn't want to because if you cripple them, they'll fall down right there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: And there could be -- there was a lot of American troops around there. And they figured it would be more dangerous to the men. But what happened is just before the Bulge broke out, they were planning for us to go closer to the frontline to shoot over the frontline at these buzz bombs. And if they crippled them, it will drop down on their territory. And they -- every time we went there, the Germans took over the position that we were supposed to set up in. And then next you knew, the Bulge broke out. And then we were in for it. I'll never forget going up into the frontline. It was a narrow two-lane road. The two-lane road was loaded with our troops retreating backwards and we couldn't even get through. I couldn't figure out why are we going forward and these guys are all going back. But we were there as a delaying action, I guess, to stop them or do something. And that was -- was the purpose of us going up there. But was it cold. Oh, I think they told me one time it was something like 30 below zero. I couldn't sleep like that now -- no how -- outside. I remember sometimes we'd have a bed roll and shake off six inches of snow in the morning. But I'll tell you one thing, I never slept in a bed roll without my shoes on. That's one thing. If I had to get out in a hurry, I wanted my shoes on my feet. And -- but it was a cold. Man, I never witnessed cold weather like that in my life. And I'm from where snow country is, but that was -- that was -- I was back there in '97 and I was talking to some lady from Netherlands. She married some GI. I guess, she was going back there for a visit. And she was telling me that was the coldest winter in history at that time. Well, a lot of boys suffered from that. Fingers, feet and toes. I remember when we went into the Bulge only ammunition I had is the 80 rounds on my belt. That's the only thing. Within a couple of days, they gave us bandoleers of ammunition, grenades and everything else. But we had never had that before -- before we went in. So -- David.

sp.speaker: Unknown male
sp.p: Coming. [Interview interrupted briefly.]

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Let's see. What else was there?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what did you do to keep warm? Anything you could do to keep warm?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Only thing we would do, we'd take over someone's farmhouse, a barn, or whatever it is and get out of the wind. That's the main thing to keep warm. That's the only thing you can do. And for people in the house, we'd tell them to get out. That's the way we -- we stayed there. You had to stay warm somehow. Sleep in the basement, sleep in the barn, sleep with the cows, anything. And Belgium people were pretty good to us. I remember one of the fellows told me at the outfit over there, they still -- still hear from some of them over there. And every time he gets a letter from them, they want to thank him what we did for them, as far as liberating their country. They did appreciate it. Belgium is strictly farm country and coal mines. I remember when we had to take a shower, we'd go down in one of these mines that these coal miners used to take showers in. That's where we would get our showers at.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So when the -- what were you doing then when the Bulge happened, when it started? You were moving forward?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: No. We were -- we were in Liege.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: And we were -- they were thinking about sending us forward to shoot these buzz bombs so that --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Buzz bombs, right.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: So that if we cripple them, they would drop on them. Since our gun had a 10-mile range, get closer to the line and -- but we didn't shoot at any -- at any of the buzz bombs. We just let them go. I remember a couple of times that they dropped close by. They were throwing them at the -- at the frontline. And I remember a corner section -- right-angle corner, it hit on the corner and you could just see the big burn mark that it -- that it hit there. See, Germans didn't use fragmentation things. They used more concussion. And it just leveled that corner. It just wiped it out. To see that thing drop and then just see the whole corner disappear. Like a whole hedgerow, you know. I guess, it's all concussion and -- but that's -- that's their warfare that they had. Where we had fragmentation ammo and bombs and grenades. Their grenades were all small things. They didn't have anything like, say, fragmentation like we did. But -- well, that's their tactics of warfare. Yeah, that's where we spent -- I think we were in there about ten days at the most in the Bulge. And then they pulled us out and back for a little rest. One thing that seemed unusual, behind us we had -- when we were in the Bulge there, we had a paratroop outfit behind us. I guess, they were reserve. If the Germans came through us, they would have met the paratroopers. But I don't know what paratroopers can do with tanks. They can't do any more than -- we were there to hold them off, which we did. And that gave the boys a chance to regroup and push them all out of Belgium.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And this would be Stoubot (ph). Can you tell me about that?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Stoumont.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Stoumont?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. That was that railroad station. A little railroad station. We went there and that's where we set up. In Battery C we had four guns. Four 90 millimeter guns. We lost three out of the four. I was on the one that remained. I was the last -- last gun. They were all in a line. And what happened is if they would have got us, they could have gone five miles without any interruption at all because our D Battery was set up behind us. But they got three out of our four, but -- we blew up the three really. They didn't capture them. We blew them up so they can't use it. But one of the things that was hard to face is they had half-tracks going along the railroad tracks. We were right on the railroad track. And they -- they can bring in infantrymen and things like that, which we weren't well prepared for that. We knew what to do with half-tracks, but what choice have you got? Yeah, we lost two of our men. I remember this one fellow named Donald Ionson (ph). He was from Iowa. He was our judo expert. Trained us for judo. And I remember him -- just before we went up to the Bulge, he got a letter from home that his brother was killed there. And I'll tell you one thing, he was bitter. And I'll bet you any amount of money that he got a couple of Germans before they got him. He was up on top of a M4 tractor. We had a 50 caliber machine gun there. And I would imagine he was just popping away at them. And what happened -- there's a weak part on a helmet of an American helmet. He hit it directly in the back. There is not much protection. The bullet will penetrate right through. That's what got him. So someone got around in back of him and -- how we know that, we found his helmet. And you could see where the bullet went right through. I mean, if you hit it on the side, it will glance off. But he got a direct hit right in the back. Well, you can't stop bullets in the head. And we lost another man. He was wounded and they tell me they picked him up, put him on a Jeep and put him back. Until today, they still don't know anything about him. He was from Ravenna, Ohio. And whatever happened to him, to this date no one knows anything about him. And I think his name was Colefield (ph). Well, fortunately, we didn't have too many casualties. It was a, like I say, cold winter. I never saw one before and never seen one since, as far as cold weather.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were you involved in the action at the rail station there or was your unit battery --

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: We were set up for them to come.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: But they never got to us. They stopped them before they got to us. You know, if you lose -- I don't know -- four or five tanks down one road, you're not going down that road anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I think if you lose four or five tanks, you probably lost half your battery of tanks.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: They didn't want to come down there. The thing of it was -- what it was is the engineers that did the -- go around the curve, you know, of a road and will put landmines across the road. And when these tanks would come around, they would kind of wiggle their way through. Well, that gave us a chance to shoot. It was about 1,000 yards down the road. Well, if you get one, the other one wants to go around him. Well, that one over there, what he did is shot first and hit the building right next to us over here. So that -- yeah. Those first three guns is the one that did the most damage. I was the one surviving gun. Like I mentioned, if they would have got by us, they would have had clear sailing for five -- five miles. There was nothing there. Our D Battery was set up behind us. But -- well, we can say that we survived that. There was another unusual thing that I remember there. They drew -- they dropped in a lot of paratroopers, spies in during the night. And I remember they gave us a serial number of a Jeep. We were, like, on a roadblock. You stop everything that goes by. And I remembered that Jeep number for many, many years, but I've lost it since. And every time a Jeep come by, we'd stop it and make sure that the serial number doesn't match with what we were told. And I read in the Stars and Stripes afterwards they caught these here German spies. They went into a motor pool in Spa, Belgium. And they had some problem with the Jeep, so they just went into the motor pool. And the guy was smart enough over there to recognize it. And what happened -- I read later on in the paper that when you -- you change uniforms, you know, you put an enemy uniform on, you're a spy. That's -- that's death. And I read in the paper where they executed them with a firing squad. And they said they had combat infantrymen doing it. Being the firing squad. And they said those boys are supposed to be so good. A lot of them missed it. That's by reading it in the paper. In the Stars and Stripes. Well, the Stars and Stripes was the only paper we had to read what was home. And that's -- I think that's about the extent of it, as far as --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What came after the Bulge then?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: We went into Heidenheim, Germany. No. We went into Remagen. That was the only bridge that was captured over the Rhine River that was intact, but that fell in anyway. And the engineers made a bridge across the Rhine River there where we crossed. And then we went to the southern Germany. I think it was called Freiburg. We stayed there only a couple of weeks or so. And that was French occupying -- French soldiers occupied zone. So we were there for a little while. And then we moved up into Heidenheim, Germany. Oh, we had a couple other stops, too. Fridingen and -- I can't even remember some of the towns. But when we were in -- the summertime there, we went to Heidenheim. We stayed there all summer long. And what we were doing at that time is picking up all these German equipment along the road or wherever it was discarded. And we would then transport it over to Munich. No. Nuremberg. And what they do there is salvage the -- the armament. They gave it to the Belgium and also the China war was going on. So they sent a lot of that equipment over to China. So after -- so after the war, we were there probably six months. And we was just going off in the field and picking up equipment -- German army equipment. In other words, get rid of it. That's the way our summer went of '45 -- '44. I'm trying to think of --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have any close buddies in the unit?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Oh, yes. I have -- there's another fellow over here on Babbitt Road.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. He was one of the gun crews that was lost. Maybe you can talk to him sometime.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Sure. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: It isn't far from here.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: If you get his name and number, I'll give him a call sometime.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Did I what?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Nothing close, no. No. I was the only one in our family, male, so -- I had a sister, but she was home here. I have a lot of pictures of the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I could look at those.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I'll show them to you.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you didn't -- you didn't see a lot of action after the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: No, no. After the Bulge, it was -- you might as well say it was over with.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I remember we went into the town called Duren.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Duren. And that's one thing about anti-aircraft -- heavy aircraft, you're close once you're behind. That's one of the good things.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: But, yeah, we -- we were behind most of the time, but so close. Close enough to where there's danger.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you get any USO shows, any entertainment?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. I saw Bob Hope there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Unfortunately, he's gone now. Yeah, I remember seeing Bob Hope. And I think it was Jean -- Jean Holcomberg (ph). I think she was with him at the time. She was a girl from Texas I remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything at all about that show?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I don't even remember where it was held. I remember they get a whole bunch of us and get them on a truck and go. I remember VJ-Day. I had a pass coming in. There was about four or five of us that went into Paris on a leave. And I remember I was in Paris on VJ-Day. That was an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Good celebrations there?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah. There was quite a bit going on. And nasty as all Americans.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: It's over with. I remember VE-Day. We were naturally into Germany at that time. And I think we were in Remagen. That was that bridge where -- the only bridge that we captured over the Rhine River. Q Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: We were up on a hillside and there was an outfit there before us. They were a 90 millimeter outfit. And, I guess, they were -- they were used as artillery -- shooting artillery over the Rhine River supporting our troops as they got over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: I got -- I can show you pictures of all the 90 millimeter shells that just piled up that they used. I still got pictures of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters and packages from home?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Oh, yes. I remember one mail call I got a letter from my sister telling me my Dad isn't well. Next letter I get, she tells me he died. Well, I didn't get home. They told me there was a war going on. I said okay. It was during -- during the Bulge. And, you know, everything was so mixed up at that time over there. Hardly any mail. They didn't get any mail from us. Some of our mail was stamped -- some of the people say they got letters delayed because -- due to enemy action. I guess, it was picked up someplace and -- I didn't get any, as far as I know. As far as home. Well, you didn't have much time to write anyway. But -- let's see. What else is there?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience, does one vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Well, I -- well, I'll say this. It's a good experience, but I would never want to do it again. I think it -- you learn to be self-sufficient, if nothing else. I'll still say that I think every fellow should be in the service, as long as there is no war. At least two years. I think that -- it will do them a lot of good. German people were nice to us. We had no problem there. One of the things we used to do is go hunting. Hunting deer there. Their deer is only about this big. Like a good-sized dog. That's all the bigger their deer were. Real small. What we used to do is take the hind quarters and front quarters and give them -- give them to the people to -- they had no food. You know, no meat. So they were glad to make that and make hamburgers or ground meat. You know, I remember there was one fellow right across the street from us over there. I used to call him Pop. And he was -- he was a soldier in the first World War. And he showed me where he got shot in the foot. And he was a nice fellow. I remember one thing. There was a girl in France gave me a silver franc coin. You very seldom found silver coins. She said that her mother gave it to her as a good luck charm and her grandmother gave it to her mother. And she gave it to me for a good luck charm. Wouldn't you know some damn fool stole it on me at home at the other house I lived?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: The mistake that I made -- I kept all these coins in one place. That was mistake number one. It was a money belt. I had all the coins in there. Well, when they're there, they saw them and took it. And that coin at that time was over 100 years old. I mean, the date -- and it was real clear the date, you know. But it was silver. I had a lot of -- all the silver coins I found, I kept them. Like the German coins, I had a lot of those with the Swastika on it. And that was a no-no after the war. They wanted no Swastika anyplace. I do have a German flag at home. I have a German army rifle. I have a German thresh (ph) sword. I've got all kind of medals, too. Q Is that stuff you collected over there?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was there a lot of souvenir collecting in the outfit?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Well, yes and no. I mean, some people did and some didn't care about it. And you were allowed to take one pistol home. I had two of them. I had a luger and a P38. And what it was is the luger I gave to a fellow that lived on the next street to me. And I worked with his brother-in-law at GE. And he told me he went out and got drunk one day and needed some money. He sold it for seven and a half dollars. The luger. It was almost as bad as what I did. I had that P38. It was a good one. It had a holster and a clip with it. And it was in good shape. I registered it here in Cleveland. And I remember the policeman that looked at it, he said, man, if you ever want to get rid of that, let me know. And my manager at work over there, he was saving P38s. He said I'll give you 195 dollars at that time. 195 dollars. This is probably 25 years ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: And I was going through a locksmithing course at that time. I figured, gee, this pistol, what am I going to do with it? I can't do anything. My wife wasn't well. My son didn't show any interest in it. I figured, hell, get rid of it. If anything happens to me, she'll probably throw it away.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: So he gave me 195 dollars. And what I did is I bought a key-cutting machine. The key-cutting machine I still use today. I'm a certified locksmith. I can make keys if I have the blanks. But that's -- see, what is a very unusual thing? I'm sure there were a lot of them, but to remember everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Anything particularly funny or strange happen?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: We had a ball team. It was a fairly decent team. We actually played all different outfits. I remember one time that -- this was fast underhand fast pitch softball. And this guy was really terrific. And I said, dog gone, I'm going to hit him. I hit him. I hit the ball right straight back at him. And the seams of the ball was shown on his stomach. I'll never forget that. So I must have hit it pretty hard. And he was a good pitcher. Hell, he struck out most of the guys. But I was determined he wasn't going to strike me out.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: So, yeah, that was -- one of the things I remember, it took me 14 days to go over. It took me 21 days to come home. I think Columbus came home faster than I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: It was that slow moving of a ship?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: It was on a lumber ship. I came home on a hospital ship. I had a little problem of passing blood. And the hospital I was in at Regensburg, Germany was a field hospital. And they said, well, they haven't got the equipment to test me. Send you back home, you'll be in the service about a month until they check you out. So they sent me on a hospital ship home. I went from Hamburg, Germany, through the English Channel and crossed. It took me 21 days -- [END OF TRACK ONE] [BEGINNING OF TRACK TWO]

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: -- to New York. I said I was determined I was going to get home. One way or the other. I told them I'm going home tonight. I want a -- they gave me an advance on my pay. And I went into Grand Central Station, took New York Central Train, and stopped right over here at the Collinwood Yards. I said that's as far as I go. I know where I'm at now. I walked this bridge many times. And I went across the street. There was a YMCA there. I called Mom. I said, I'll be home. I said, I'll be home shortly. Where are you? I said, I'll be home shortly. It took me about five minutes to walk home from there. So I went home. It was something strange to come home. You know you're not going to see Dad again.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: But I did get home. And then I had to come back and then I had to go to a hospital in Staten Island. And I was only there for a couple of days. And then they sent me down to White Sulfur Springs in West Virginia. And that's a -- it's a palace. Plus, they want to keep you. One doctor I met over there, he says, I'll tell you what, most of these doctors here are -- are career doctors. They want to stay in the service. And they were in charge of field hospitals. And he says, and they got to get the practice now. He said, don't let them practice on you. Every morning I answered roll call and I said I want out, out. After about a week of that, they sent me home to Indianapolis. I went home. That ended my career. But it was a beautiful place down in West Sulfur Springs. I think that's where the Japanese envoys were when they were coming here to talk peace before -- before they attacked Pearl Harbor. They were at that hotel. It's a beautiful resort. I think that Sammy Snead is a -- that's where he played golf. I think that's where it is, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's in West Virginia or Maryland?

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: West Virginia, uh-huh. White Sulfur Springs. That's what it was called, yeah. Yeah, that's a beautiful place. I've been down there once since then. But like after you go there 25 years later, heck, you can't even recognize the place anymore. Some of the things I remember, but I think there is two 18-hole golf courses and one nine in that area there. It's mostly for golf. Let's see. I'm just trying to think of -- what other unusual thing. I remember when we left California for New York that was another five day trip on a train. We were home a month before that. They gave us a furlough. They told us that we will be going overseas. I didn't know if we were going to go to the Pacific or to Europe. I kind of figured Pacific because we took our training out in the desert, you know. I figured I would be there, but, no, went to Europe and froze to death there. I remember another thing that -- when I went to Europe in '97, I saw the Eiffel Tower. And I saw it, naturally, during the war. And one big difference, there was -- at that time and the time we were there, it was all lit up. During the war, you know, that's -- that was never lit up. I guess, it's -- would be a landmark so they didn't -- they didn't have it lit up at all there. But we -- we had a -- I took the Hovercraft from England -- from France to England, then I went on to London and boarded a plane and came home. The reason I took that trip, I was never in London, was never in Holland, was never in Rome. And that trip went through that. We went through Paris. Well, I had been in Paris. But, you know, after 25 years it's hard to remember any of that stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: It does come back to you a little bit, but -- at the Eiffel Tower and Arc de Triomphe yeah. Well, yeah, we -- it was quite an experience. As far as action, we were fortunate. We didn't get into too much of it. I would say that I was -- I was fortunate and the dear Lord was with me. Like I was saying, buzz bombs dropping all around you. I remember one time -- one place in Belgium we were staying in and it used to be every other night half the crew would go into town, go to bars, drink beer or something, you know. And all of a sudden, we moved out. And that was the night that I was supposed to go to the bar. I'd go to the bar. Here, a buzz bomb dropped right on the thing and killed everybody in there. I remember there was one colored American soldier that was there. He used to be there every night. And he got killed. You know, I think I was just one step ahead of it all the whole time, I guess. You just -- you do or you don't, that's all. I was fortunate. I'm sure a lot -- I talk to a lot of those fellows. I remember some of those combat infantrymen. I got a GI compass from one of these fellows that was -- I met in the hospital when I was in Germany there. He gave me one of his compasses, as far as a remembrance. And I gave him something. I forget now what it was. But he gave me this compass. I have it. It's a GI compass. And he said, Joe, if this thing could talk, he could tell you a lot of stories. And I imagine it could. You know, being a combat infantryman.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph John Dvorabic
sp.p: Yeah, those poor guys. They went in first. You know, how the hell you survive that? [Audio ends and begins repeating track two.]
